questions.q: In the Customer 360 case study, why is product-usage telemetry a strong candidate for data virtualization rather than replication?
options: Because it is enormous in volume, changes constantly, and is only occasionally viewed by a rep — replicating that much rarely-viewed data into Salesforce storage would be wasteful
Because telemetry data is small in volume and rarely changes
Because telemetry data cannot be accessed through any API
Because virtualized data is always more accurate than replicated data
questions.explain: Telemetry's high volume, constant change rate, and infrequent viewing make it a poor fit for full replication — exactly the profile Lesson 14 identifies as favoring virtualization, which avoids storing large amounts of data that's rarely actually queried.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend billing status be replicated into Salesforce rather than virtualized?
options: Because billing data changes too frequently to replicate
Because billing data is never looked at by reps
Because the finance system has no API available at all
Because reps need it to be fast and reliably available even if the finance system is briefly down for maintenance
questions.explain: Billing status needs to be fast and available even during a brief finance-system outage — exactly the availability concern that favors replication (via scheduled delta sync) over virtualization's real-time dependency on the source system.

questions.q: Why does the legacy ticketing tool's scheduled retirement affect the integration approach chosen for it, per this lesson?
options: It doesn't affect the approach at all; retirement timing is irrelevant to integration design
Investing in a clean virtualization adapter for a system that will soon be decommissioned has a short shelf life, so a simpler, lower-investment integration may be the pragmatic choice
Legacy systems can never be integrated with Salesforce Connect under any circumstances
A system scheduled for retirement must always be fully replicated immediately
questions.explain: Pattern choice also has to account for a source system's own expected lifespan — building a sophisticated virtualization adapter for a system that will soon be retired may not be worth the investment, favoring a simpler, lower-cost integration instead.

questions.q: In the API-led connectivity design for this case study, what does the Process API do?
options: It directly stores all customer data permanently, replacing the need for any System APIs
It replaces the need for any Experience-layer component
It combines the finance, telemetry, and ticketing System APIs' outputs into one assembled "customer health summary" response for the Experience layer to call
It is only used for authentication, not for data assembly
questions.explain: The Process API sits above the three System APIs, combining their individual outputs into one assembled response — the layer the Salesforce-side component calls instead of calling all three backends separately and assembling the view itself.

questions.q: What problem does master data management (MDM) and the golden record concept address?
options: It addresses what happens when multiple systems hold conflicting copies of the same data element, by designating a defined, non-arbitrary authoritative source for each element
It addresses network latency between systems
It addresses how to choose between synchronous and asynchronous communication
It is only relevant to Bulk API batch jobs
questions.explain: MDM exists specifically to resolve disagreement when the same data element exists in multiple systems — designating a golden-record source for each element so there's a defined rule for which value wins, rather than guesswork or silent overwrites.
